features.headline: NFC North: Bears win division? Cousins has Vikes in command?
features.desc: What will Kirk Cousins and Micah Parsons mean for the best division in football, or will the Bears hang on?
features.by: Courtney Cronin and Rob Demovsky and Kevin Seifert and Eric Woodyard
body: No one in the NFL was on a bigger high coming out of last weekend than the Green Bay Packers.
They trounced the defending AFC champion New England Patriots 45-27 and put together their best performance of the season to improve to 6-3.
And then Packers coach Matt LaFleur killed the buzz: "The reality is this: We're in last place in our division right now."
Such is life in the NFC North, the most victorious division in football, where the Chicago Bears are on top at 7-3, followed by the Detroit Lions (6-2), Minnesota Vikings (6-2) and Packers (6-3).

The NFC North is the seventh division since 2002 with all four teams above.500 through Week 9, according to ESPN Research. It has the best combined record (25-9, 73.5 winning percentage) by any division in the first nine weeks of a season under the current division format, which began 24 years ago.

The last time all four teams in a division had a winning record at this point in a season was 2023 with the AFC North. All four finished with winning records, and all but the Cincinnati Bengals (9-8) made the playoffs. The Baltimore Ravens made it to the AFC Championship Game.

On the flip side of that was the 2022 AFC East, which also had every team with a winning record through Week 9 but had only two teams reach the playoffs, and neither advanced past the divisional round.
ESPN's FPI gives the Bears the best shot at winning the division at 35.1%, ahead of the Vikings (29.7%), Lions (24.7%) and Packers (10.5%).
So what's real and what's not in the NFC North? Reporters Courtney Cronin (Bears), Rob Demovsky (Packers), Kevin Seifert (Vikings) and Eric Woodyard (Lions) give their insight:

features.headline: It's a battle for the AFC North: Steelers at Bengals Week 10 primer
features.desc: Aaron Rodgers and Joe Burrow and their 6-2 teams face off Sunday night, and Ben Baby and Brooke Pryor break down the matchup.
body: Pittsburgh Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham arrived at his news conference a few minutes late Monday afternoon.
"Sorry about that," he said as he stepped behind the lectern. "Tee Higgins, Joe Burrow, [Ja'Marr] Chase, a lot of guys."
He laughed and shook his head as a reporter asked if anything was different from their first matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals nearly two months earlier — a 30-27 win in Week 3.

It's a matchup that would give any defensive coordinator nightmares, and Sunday night in Cincinnati (8:20 ET, NBC) the chess game between the Bengals' high-flying offense and the Steelers' stalwart, veteran-laden defense clashes again with high stakes.
The winner of Sunday's rematch will move into first place in the AFC North. For the Steelers, a win will mean a crucial division sweep of the Bengals to maintain their tiebreak advantage.
For the Bengals, a victory will even the 2026 series with the Steelers with three division games left — including two against the frisky Cleveland Browns.
"I love playing in primetime," Burrow said. "Some guys would rather play at 1 [p.m.].

I'd rather play every game [on] Sunday night, 'Monday Night Football.' I want to be able to showcase what we do and how hard we work and go and showcase what we can do to the world. And this is a big moment for it."
Burrow, though, has never played in a home divisional primetime game. On the other side, the Steelers haven't won a road divisional primetime game since 2024.
Since their September meeting, each team has lost once, and both enter the matchup riding a four-game winning streak.

features.headline: Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders' sit-and-learn plan: Is he ready to start?
features.desc: The Raiders had a plan for Fernando Mendoza in Year 1 and stuck to it as long as they could. But he's now QB1 earlier than expected, and they have to trust he's ready.
body: The day you find out you're going to be a parent is one of the scariest days of your life. It comes with all the worries, from the mundane and practical (What if I drop him?) to the broad and existential (What if I mess him up?).
All of it comes under the terrifying umbrella of "What if I'm not ready?"
The fact is you're probably not, and you probably never will be.

This thought popped into my head Tuesday, when the Raiders' deadline-day trade of Kirk Cousins to the Vikings suddenly elevated rookie Fernando Mendoza into the role of starting quarterback — sooner than the team had planned. Is he ready?
Maybe not, but that's not the relevant question anymore. It's happening, and all the Raiders can do is try their best to not mess this up.

"It shouldn't be a whirlwind if he's been preparing the right way each week," Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said Thursday. "At some point, he knew he was going to get an opportunity, and so he's been preparing that way since April."

Sure, sounds great. Mendoza was the first pick in the 2026 draft as a Heisman Trophy winner and national champion. He's comfortable in the spotlight and has a history of exceeding expectations. He might be absolutely fine from the jump.

He might have been fine if the Raiders had never signed Cousins and they had started him in Week 1, the way the Titans did with Cam Ward last season, the Bears did with Caleb Williams the year before that, the Panthers did with Bryce Young the year before that, and so on.

All of those guys had plenty of hiccups at the start — there aren't a lot of Joe Burrows or Andrew Lucks out there who get picked No. 1 and hit right away — but there's also no real evidence that starting right away is the reason Young and Ward are still struggling, or that Williams is lighting up the league in Year 3.

features.headline: Is Chuba Hubbard the biggest X factor to spark a Panthers turnaround?
features.desc: Meet Carolina's team captain, a locker room leader and a relentless running back who is "chasing greatness myself."
body: CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Chuba Hubbard knows that no one is perfect. But that hasn't stopped the Carolina Panthers' running back from chasing perfection.

And after a forgettable, injury-marred 2025 campaign, during which he lost his starting job after a career season in 2024, the team captain is leading the backfield again, and he's perhaps better than ever.

"I pride myself in hard work and staying consistent in knowing what I can do and trying to bring my best every single day, so it's more so just fighting for excellence and fighting to be perfect in every way possible," Hubbard told ESPN.
Hubbard, 27, signed a four-year, $33.2 million contract extension during his breakout 2024 campaign, when he rushed for 1,195 yards and produced 11 total touchdowns in 15 games.

Through eight games in 2026, he has rushed for 619 yards and produced seven total touchdowns, bouncing back as the Panthers have struggled to find consistency almost everywhere else during a three-game losing streak and a 3-5 start.
But those numbers don't tell the complete story of Hubbard's value. He's talented, sure, but his true worth is as a tone-setter for the organization.

Though he was selected by the franchise, while Matt Rhule was the coach, in the fourth round of the 2021 NFL draft, Hubbard has established himself as the standard-bearer for the Dave Canales era over the past three seasons.
And with Carolina fighting to maintain its position atop the NFC South, his value has become apparent, if not paramount, to the team's ability to recalibrate its season.

features.headline: How Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong became unanimous NL MVP
features.desc: The Cubs' star center fielder hit another level midway through the 2026 season. Here's what shaped PCA's superstar turn.
body: It's easy to forget that Pete Crow-Armstrong was having a quiet first six weeks of the 2026 MLB season after signing a six-year, $115 million contract extension a few months earlier.

The moment that turned the Chicago Cubs center fielder into a runaway favorite for National League MVP honors — and eventual unanimous winner — didn't come until mid-May, in a matchup against the Atlanta Braves and 2024 Cy Young winner Chris Sale.

Crow-Armstrong's defense, as usual, had been outstanding. But while batting ninth in the order during the early portion of the year, he had yet to find his groove at the plate and was batting just.238 with a.679 OPS.
Cubs hitting coach John Mallee attempted a "we have nothing to lose moment" against the nasty left-hander. The Cubs decided to move the lefty-hitting Crow-Armstrong closer to the plate.
"You're either going to get hit or the ball's going forward," Mallee recalled saying to Crow-Armstrong going into the game. "There's only two options because you're standing on top of the plate now."
It was similar to what former Cubs star Anthony Rizzo tried years earlier under Mallee's tutelage.

Back then, when Mallee expressed concern for Rizzo's health — as his hit by pitch totals increased — the former All-Star first baseman famously reminded Mallee that he had survived cancer so he wasn't much afraid of a baseball.
Crow-Armstrong decided he was up for the challenge after talking to Rizzo about it. He wanted to get on base more. Getting hit was one way.

Crow-Armstrong didn't get hit, but he did go 1-for-2 off Sale that day. He turned on a 97 mph pitch for a single in the second then grounded out on a 3-1 count in the fifth. They were not headline generating plays, but they were the genesis for the months filled with such moments ahead.

features.headline: Who has won the MLB MVP Award? All-time winners list
features.desc: MLB's MVP Award is given to top players in the American League and National League. Take a look at the all-time winners list now.
body: There are two MVPs in Major League Baseball each year — one in the American League and one in the National League. Since 1931, the Baseball Writers' Association of America has voted for the MVPs at the end of the regular season and before the start of the postseason.
The award began in 1911 as the Chalmers Award, honoring the "most important and useful player to the club and to the league." That award was discontinued in 1914.

From 1922 to 1928 in the AL and from 1924 to 1929 in the NL, the League Award was presented to "the baseball player who is of the greatest all-around service to his club." Prior winners were not eligible to win the award again during that time.

In 2026, Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros won MVP for the American League, the 3rd Astros player to win the award after Jose Altuve in 2017 and Jeff Bagwell in 1994. Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs won for the National League, the first Cubs player to win it since Kris Bryant in 2016.
Take a look at all-time AL and NL MVP award winners below:
2026: Yordan Alvarez (AL), Pete Crow-Armstrong (NL)
2023: Shohei Ohtani (AL), Ronald Acuna Jr. (NL)
2022: Aaron Judge (AL), Paul Goldschmidt (NL)
2018: Mookie Betts (AL), Christian Yelich (NL)
2017: Jose Altuve (AL), Giancarlo Stanton (NL)
2013: Miguel Cabrera (AL), Andrew McCutchen (NL)
2008: Dustin Pedroia (AL), Albert Pujols (NL)
2007: Alex Rodriguez (AL), Jimmy Rollins (NL)
2005: Alex Rodriguez (AL), Albert Pujols (NL)
2004: Vladimir Guerrero (AL), Barry Bonds (NL)
1999: Iván Rodríguez (AL), Chipper Jones (NL)
